email-header-analyzer.title: Email Header Analyzer
email-header-analyzer.summary: Paste the headers of a suspicious email to see where it really came from, which authentication checks it passed and what looks suspicious. Runs locally in your browser; internal IP addresses, addresses and server names never leave it. No finding does not mean a message is safe.
email-header-analyzer.how_it_works:
The headers of an email record its journey: every mail server adds a Received line, and the receiving server records whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC passed. Online header analyzers ask you to upload those headers, with your internal addresses and server names. This tool reads them in your browser instead.

Path: Received lines are read from the sender to you, with server names, IP addresses, times and delays. The tool marks the trust boundary: lines above it were added by your own servers; everything below the first external server could have been written by the sender. Enter your domain to set the boundary precisely.

Authentication: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC results are shown with the server that recorded them; results written below the boundary or by an unknown server are marked as not trusted. Alignment compares the From domain with the SPF and DKIM domains, using the Public Suffix List for organizational domains.

Warning signs: display names that name another address or a brand, Reply-To on another domain, lookalike domains (punycode, mixed alphabets, digits for letters) and unusual Date or Message-ID.
email-header-analyzer.documentation:
Input

Paste the headers or the whole message source, or open a saved .eml or .txt file, up to 5 MB. Only the part before the first empty line is analysed; the body and attachments are ignored and never shown or exported.

Output

Findings with severity, explanation and what to check next; the delivery path with the trust boundary; authentication results with their trust; alignment. Download as Markdown or JSON, optionally with recipient addresses and internal IPs masked.

No lookups

The tool does not query DNS, WHOIS or reputation services and does not verify DKIM signatures; it shows what the receiving servers recorded.

Data

Public Suffix List from publicsuffix.org (Mozilla Public License 2.0), list of 2026-11-17, published unmodified with its license text.
email-header-analyzer.examples:
A message that claims to be from PayPal

From: "PayPal Service" <service@paypa1-billing.example>
Authentication-Results: mx.example.com; dmarc=fail
→ HIGH Lookalike domain · HIGH Claims a brand and fails authentication

A forged result

A second Authentication-Results line saying “pass”, written below your server’s own line, is shown as not trusted.
email-header-analyzer.faq:
Are my headers sent anywhere?

No. This tool does not transmit the text you enter. There are no DNS, WHOIS or reputation lookups; everything runs in your browser tab.

Does “no warning signs” mean the email is genuine?

No. No known warning signs matched does not mean the message is safe. A hijacked real account, or a message sent through a legitimate service, passes every check.

Why are some results marked as not trusted?

Anyone can write an Authentication-Results line. Only lines added by your own mail servers, above the trust boundary, can be believed.

Is the message body analysed?

No. The body, links and attachments are ignored and never included in the report.
